name: Interdisciplinary pain rehabilitation / functional restoration (Mayo Clinic Pain Rehabilitation Center and similar)
founders: Barbara K. Bruce (led development of Mayo pediatric PRC, 2008)
Wesley Gilliam, Jeannie Sperry, Cynthia Townsend, W. Michael Hooten, Jeffrey Rome (Mayo PRC clinicians and investigators)
Wilbert E. Fordyce (operant pain programs, University of Washington, 1968-76)
Tom Mayer and Robert Gatchel (functional restoration, PRIDE Dallas, 1980s)
founded_year_range: 1974 for the Mayo Rochester PRC, per Mayo's site ("one of the first pain rehabilitation programs in the world"; Mayo-sourced only). Generic model 1960-1987: Bonica clinic; Fordyce operant work 1968, book 1976; Mayer/Gatchel functional restoration JAMA 1987. Mayo expansions: pediatric Oct 2008, Florida 2011, Arizona 2016.
delivery: intensive outpatient day program (3 weeks, ~8 h/day; pediatric 17 days)
cost_summary: Price not published. KFF Health News/NPR (2017) reported the Mayo 3-week program 'can cost up to $40,000' for patients with complicated medical problems, mostly billed to insurance; very few pay out of pocket. One Mayo Clinic Connect report of ~USD 52k is anecdotal (page blocked to automated access, no archive). Mayo's PRC costs-and-insurance page (Wayback, Apr 2025) gives no price. Three weeks of travel and lodging are paid by the patient. Typical-cost figure below is an estimate.
mechanisms: autonomic/nervous system dysregulation (sympathetic overdrive, "stuck in fight-or-flight")
mechanism_summary: Biopsychosocial and agnostic about ultimate etiology. Disability is maintained by operantly reinforced pain behaviours (Fordyce), fear-avoidance and catastrophizing, deconditioning (the Mayer/Gatchel "deconditioning syndrome"), and symptom-driven medications (opioids, benzodiazepines; opioid-induced hyperalgesia), with central sensitization and stress/autonomic arousal as modulators. Pediatric POTS disability is framed as partly maintained by deconditioning, symptom focus and family accommodation. The goal is function, not cure.
techniques: 3-week intensive outpatient day program (~120 contact hours, estimated)
group pain education using CBT/ACT (self-regulation, stress management, problem-solving, cognitive restructuring)
daily physical therapy: aerobic conditioning, strengthening, stretching, body mechanics
extinction of pain behaviours / reinforcement of well behaviours
occupational therapy: pacing, activity scheduling, return to valued roles and work
biofeedback, diaphragmatic breathing, progressive muscle relaxation
supervised taper of opioids, benzodiazepines, muscle relaxants and other symptom-driven medications
nursing education on sleep, nutrition, smoking
graded upright tolerance and reconditioning for POTS (pediatric)
mainstream_notes: Archetypal tertiary pain-care model with CARF accreditation standards, Cochrane reviews and NICE NG59 recommendation (combined physical and psychological programme for persistent low back pain with psychosocial obstacles); operationalises CDC/VA nonpharmacological care and opioid tapering. VA CARF programs grew from 2 to 20 (2009-2019; Murphy et al. Pain Med 2021). Widespread in Germany (multimodal pain therapy) and Scandinavia. In US private care, CARF-accredited programs fell from 210 (1998) to 87 (2019) per CARF International data (Murphy et al. 2021; Haun et al. 2025), with other tallies of 84 (2005) and ~54 (2022, presentation), mainly because of reimbursement; some programs dropped accreditation without closing. Pediatric IIPT runs at Mayo, Boston Children's, Cincinnati (FIRST), Stanford and Datteln, among others.
insurance_notes: Commonly covered by commercial insurers and (per patient reports) Medicare as outpatient rehabilitation/psychology services or program per diem, usually with prior authorisation. Denials as "not medically necessary" are common, and Mayo's insurance team advocates case by case (KFF Health News 2017). A Mayo Florida-Florida Blue pre-post cost study (Sletten 2015, n=53) reported 64-90% lower medical costs after treatment.

key_trials.citation: Kamper SJ et al. Multidisciplinary biopsychosocial rehabilitation for chronic low back pain: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 2015;350:h444
key_trials.design: Systematic review/meta-analysis of 41 RCTs (generic model, not Mayo)
key_trials.finding: Versus usual care: pain SMD 0.21 (~0.5/10 points) and disability SMD 0.23 (moderate quality). Versus physical treatment: pain SMD 0.51 (CI crosses 0) and disability SMD 0.68 (low quality, heterogeneous). Better odds of working at 1 year than physical treatment (OR 1.87) but not than usual care (OR 1.04).

key_trials.citation: Guzman J et al. Multidisciplinary rehabilitation for chronic low back pain: systematic review. BMJ 2001;322:1511-6
key_trials.finding: Strong evidence that intensive biopsychosocial rehabilitation with functional restoration improves function, and moderate evidence that it reduces pain; contradictory vocational evidence. Less intensive programs were ineffective.

key_trials.citation: Flor H, Fydrich T, Turk DC. Efficacy of multidisciplinary pain treatment centers: a meta-analytic review. Pain 1992;49:221-30
key_trials.finding: Superior to no treatment, waitlist and single-discipline care for pain, mood, return to work and healthcare use, with stable effects. Study quality was marginal.

key_trials.citation: Mayer TG et al. A prospective two-year study of functional restoration in industrial low back injury. JAMA 1987;258:1763-7
key_trials.design: Prospective non-randomized controlled cohort (116 treated vs 72 untreated)
key_trials.finding: At 2 years, 87% of treated patients were working vs 41% of untreated comparisons; comparison group had about twice as much additional spine surgery.

key_trials.citation: Hechler T et al. Inpatient-based intensive interdisciplinary pain treatment for highly impaired children with severe chronic pain: RCT of efficacy and economic effects. Pain 2014;155:118-28
key_trials.design: RCT vs waitlist (German pediatric IIPT, Datteln)
key_trials.finding: 55% vs 14% improved at post-treatment. Disability, school absence, depression and catastrophizing improved immediately; pain intensity and anxiety improved only by short-term follow-up.

key_trials.citation: Hechler T et al. Systematic review on intensive interdisciplinary pain treatment of children with chronic pain. Pediatrics 2015;136:115-27
key_trials.finding: Large post-treatment improvement in disability, small-to-moderate in pain and depression, maintained at short-term follow-up; extreme heterogeneity.

key_trials.citation: Claus BB et al. Intensive interdisciplinary pain treatment for children and adolescents with chronic noncancer pain: preregistered systematic review and IPD meta-analysis. Pain 2022;163:2281-2301
key_trials.design: Individual-patient-data meta-analysis, 13 sites (pre-post designs; includes Mayo co-author)
key_trials.finding: Large improvements in pain (g=-1.28), disability (g=-1.91) and missed school (g=-0.99, 12-month follow-up); moderate improvements in anxiety (g=-0.77) and depression (g=-0.76). Certainty very low to low.

key_trials.citation: Townsend CO et al. A longitudinal study of the efficacy of a comprehensive pain rehabilitation program with opioid withdrawal. Pain 2008;140:177-89
key_trials.design: Mayo uncontrolled longitudinal cohort (admission, discharge, 6 months)
key_trials.finding: 91% completed; 70% of completers returned 6-month data. All outcomes improved at discharge and 6 months regardless of opioid use at admission (57% on daily opioids), after opioid withdrawal.

key_trials.citation: Hooten WM et al. Treatment outcomes after multidisciplinary pain rehabilitation with analgesic medication withdrawal for patients with fibromyalgia. Pain Med 2007;8:8-16
key_trials.finding: MPI, SF-36, catastrophizing and depression improved, and opioid, NSAID, benzodiazepine and muscle-relaxant use fell at dismissal.

key_trials.citation: Bruce BK et al. Development of an interdisciplinary pediatric pain rehabilitation program: the first 1000 consecutive patients. Mayo Clin Proc Innov Qual Outcomes 2017;1:141-9
key_trials.finding: Functional disability fell from 27 to 9, depression from 27 to 14 and catastrophizing from 26 to 14. Of the 16% on opioids, all but 4 tapered off.

key_trials.citation: Bruce BK et al. Improvement in functioning and psychological distress in adolescents with POTS following interdisciplinary treatment. Clin Pediatr 2016;55:1300-4
key_trials.finding: Adolescents with POTS improved in functional ability and had lower depression and catastrophizing after the 3-week program.

key_trials.citation: Sletten CD et al. Economic analysis of a comprehensive pain rehabilitation program: Florida Blue and Mayo Clinic Florida. Pain Med 2015;16:898-904
key_trials.finding: Medical costs fell 86%, 68%, 64% and 90% at 3, 6, 12 and 18 months after treatment vs matched pre-treatment periods.

controversy: Mandatory opioid and benzodiazepine tapering is seen by some as coercive, a concern sharpened by the CDC 2022 warnings against forced/abrupt tapers. Operant "ignoring" of pain behaviour can feel invalidating. Rehabilitative framing of pediatric POTS and fatigue, and graded activity, are contested by POTS and ME/CFS communities (NICE NG206 on graded exercise therapy). The program is costly, insurers often deny it, and US access is limited after program closures. Mayo's evidence is in-house uncontrolled cohorts with no RCT of the Mayo program, and effects against usual care in RCTs of the generic model are small.

indicators.metric: Mayo Rochester adult PRC annual patients
indicators.value: >300 per year; >80% completion despite required opioid taper; program described as 40 years old

indicators.source: Bruce et al. 2017 Mayo Clin Proc Innov Qual Outcomes
Murphy et al. Pain Med 2021 (PMC8599775), citing CARF International; Haun et al. JMIR Res Protoc 2025 (PMC12089867); CARF/VA presentation; IntechOpen chapter 2021
Murphy et al., Pain Med 2021 (IASP-linked summary)

popularity.reach_estimate: Mayo PRCs alone: ~300+/yr in Rochester for ~50 years, plus Florida, Arizona and pediatric programs, giving roughly 20,000-30,000 cumulative patients (log10 ~4.4). The generic interdisciplinary/multimodal model (US peak era, VA, Germany, Scandinavia, pediatric IIPT) has plausibly reached on the order of 1 million people worldwide (log10 ~6); this broader figure is used here but is a rough, unverified extrapolation.
popularity.method_notes: Trajectory reflects the generic interdisciplinary model, anchored on Mayo. Rise from Bonica and Fordyce (1968-76) and Mayo 1974; peak in the 1985-1998 functional-restoration/CARF era; decline as CARF-accredited programs fell from 210 (1998) to 84 by 2005 and 87 by 2019 (peer-reviewed sources date the 210 figure to 1998; a '>1000 US clinics' figure sometimes attributed to Schatman was not found in PubMed, Europe PMC full text or the VA papers and is not used); partial revival with Mayo expansions (2008-2016), pediatric IIPT and opioid-crisis attention (CDC 2016, KFF/NPR 2017, VA tenfold growth); steady through the 2020s. Reach is a rough order-of-magnitude estimate from Mayo throughput (300+/yr) extrapolated to many programs internationally; it does not count German multimodal therapy separately (no verified figures). Google Trends was not used, and Reddit's API blocked automated access (2026-10-13); this is a clinic-based model with little social-media footprint beyond Mayo Clinic Connect threads.
